primary_meaning: An outsider or alien—especially someone separated from God’s covenant people, but capable of being welcomed and incorporated into the community. In many passages “stranger” is first a literal social category rather than a fixed symbol; Christian interpretation often extends it to spiritual alienation and reconciliation.
primary_basis: Ephesians 2:12, 19 — Gentiles were “strangers to the covenants of promise” but become members of God’s household.
Leviticus 19:33–34 — Israel must love the stranger residing among them as themselves.
Deuteronomy 10:18–19 — God loves the stranger, and Israel is commanded to do likewise.
Isaiah 56:3–8 — foreigners who join themselves to the Lord are welcomed among God’s people.
Colossians 1:21–22 — alienation from God followed by reconciliation, although many translations do not use “stranger.”

alternatives.meaning: The believer as a pilgrim or temporary resident in the present world, whose true homeland is heavenly.
basis: Hebrews 11:13–16 — the faithful confess that they are strangers and pilgrims on earth and seek a heavenly country.
1 Peter 2:11 — Christians are addressed as strangers, exiles, or sojourners.
Philippians 3:20 — believers’ citizenship is in heaven.

alternatives.meaning: The vulnerable outsider in whom Christ is encountered and to whom hospitality and mercy must be shown.
basis: Matthew 25:35, 38, 43–45 — welcoming the stranger is treated as welcoming Christ.
Hebrews 13:2 — hospitality to strangers may amount to entertaining angels.
Luke 10:25–37 — the outsider becomes the exemplary neighbor, though the word “stranger” is not the central term.

alternatives.meaning: A person whose voice or teaching does not belong to Christ, and whom Christ’s sheep therefore refuse to follow.
basis: John 10:5 — the sheep flee from a stranger because they do not recognize the stranger’s voice.
John 10:1–10 — the surrounding shepherd imagery associates unauthorized figures with danger to the flock.

alternatives.meaning: Christ himself as unrecognized, rejected, or apparently foreign to those he visits.
basis: Matthew 25:35–40 — Christ identifies himself with the stranger who is welcomed.
Luke 24:18 — the risen Jesus is initially treated as a stranger by the disciples on the Emmaus road.
John 1:10–11 — Christ comes to his own but is not received, though “stranger” is not explicitly used.

notes: There is no single settled biblical symbolism for “stranger.” The term often denotes an actual foreigner, resident alien, guest, or unknown person. Its meaning also varies with the underlying Hebrew and Greek terms, including ger (resident alien/sojourner), nokri (foreigner), xenos (stranger/foreigner), and paroikos (sojourner). The outsider or alien is the broadest recurring theological association, while the pilgrim-believer and Christ-in-the-stranger readings are also well established.
